```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(fixedincome)
```

Interest rates are quoted per year, but money is lent for some number of days.
To compound a rate we need the period in years, and the day count convention
(the *daycount*) is the rule that turns a period between two dates into a
fraction of a year.

The same annual rate, for the same two dates, gives different amounts of
interest with different daycounts.
That is why every `SpotRate` in `fixedincome` carries its daycount.

## How a daycount works

A daycount has two parts, written as `"<days>/<days in base>"`:

- how the **days** between two dates are counted: actual days, business days,
  or 30 days per month;
- the **days in base**: how many of these days make one year.

The year fraction is the number of days divided by the days in base.

```{r}
dc <- daycount("actual/360")
dc
dib(dc)
```

`fixedincome` supports these daycounts:

| Daycount | Days counted | Days in base | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `actual/360` | calendar days | 360 | money markets in USD and EUR |
| `actual/365` | calendar days | 365 | GBP money markets, many bonds |
| `business/252` | business days | 252 | Brazilian rates (DI, Selic, bonds) |
| `30E/360` | 30 days per month | 360 | Eurobonds |

Other bases also work with `actual` and `business`, for example
`actual/366` or `business/250`.

## Counting the days between two dates

For `actual/...` and `business/...` the days are counted with the **calendar**
of the rate, using the [bizdays](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=bizdays)
package.
The `"actual"` calendar counts every day, and `"Brazil/ANBIMA"` counts only
business days in Brazil.

```{r}
d1 <- as.Date("2024-01-31")
d2 <- as.Date("2024-07-31")
term(d1, d2, "actual")
term(d1, d2, "Brazil/ANBIMA")
```

With `30E/360` every month has 30 days, and a date on the 31st is moved to
the 30th, so from 2024-01-31 to 2024-07-31 there are exactly 6 × 30 = 180
days.
The calendar is not used.

## Same rate, different daycounts

Let's compound a simple rate of 10% from `d1` to `d2` with each daycount.

```{r}
compound(spotrate(0.10, "simple", "actual/360", "actual"), d1, d2)
compound(spotrate(0.10, "simple", "actual/365", "actual"), d1, d2)
compound(spotrate(0.10, "simple", "business/252", "Brazil/ANBIMA"), d1, d2)
compound(spotrate(0.10, "simple", "30E/360", "actual"), d1, d2)
```

The year fractions are 182/360, 182/365, 125/252 and 180/360.
So `actual/360` pays the most interest: it counts every day, but its year
has only 360 days.
A rate of 10% is not the same rate under different daycounts.

## Equivalent rates

To compare rates with different daycounts, find the rate that gives the same
compounding factor for the same dates.
`implied_rate()` returns the rate for a compounding factor and a year
fraction.

Here a Brazilian rate of 10% (`business/252`) is converted to an
`actual/365` rate for the same period.

```{r}
sr <- spotrate(0.10, "discrete", "business/252", "Brazil/ANBIMA")
factor <- compound(sr, d1, d2)
factor

years <- as.numeric(term(d1, d2, "actual")) / 365
rate <- implied_rate("discrete", years, factor)
sr365 <- spotrate(rate, "discrete", "actual/365", "actual")
sr365
compound(sr365, d1, d2)
```

Both rates give the same factor for these dates, but the equivalent rate
depends on the dates: another period has another number of business days.

## Rates for other periods

`SpotRate` objects are always annual, but many rates are quoted for other
periods: inflation per month, the DI rate per day, coupons per semester.
The `period` argument of `spotrate()` takes the rate for one period and
stores the equivalent annual rate: the rate with the same compounding factor
over that period.
The period is a `Term`, or a string like `"1 month"`, and the daycount of
the rate turns it into a fraction of a year.

```{r}
inflation <- spotrate(0.0045, "discrete", "business/252", "Brazil/ANBIMA",
  period = "1 month"
)
inflation
compound(inflation, term(1, "month"))
```

With `business/252` one month is 21 business days, but calendar months have
17 to 23 business days in Brazil.
For a rate tied to a specific month, use a `Term` created from two dates:
the rate is converted with the business days of that month, so compounding
between those dates gives back the monthly rate.

```{r}
jan <- term(as.Date("2024-01-01"), as.Date("2024-02-01"), "Brazil/ANBIMA")
jan
inflation_jan <- spotrate(0.0045, "discrete", "business/252", "Brazil/ANBIMA",
  period = jan
)
compound(inflation_jan, as.Date("2024-01-01"), as.Date("2024-02-01"))
```

## Real interest rates

The real rate is the nominal rate discounted by inflation:
$(1 + \text{real}) = (1 + \text{nominal}) / (1 + \text{inflation})$.
With discrete compounding this holds for any period, so it can be computed
directly with annual `SpotRate` objects that have the same compounding,
daycount and calendar.

```{r}
nominal <- spotrate(0.1065, "discrete", "business/252", "Brazil/ANBIMA")
real <- (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1
real
```

The real rate for one month is the same with both ways of computing it.

```{r}
compound(real, term(1, "month")) - 1
compound(nominal, term(1, "month")) / compound(inflation, term(1, "month")) - 1
```

## Converting Terms

A `Term` can be in days, months or years, and the daycount says how many days
there are in one year (or in one month, which is one twelfth of a year).
`todays()`, `tomonths()` and `toyears()` convert Terms with a daycount.

```{r}
todays(daycount("business/252"), term(1, "year"))
todays(daycount("actual/365"), term(1, "year"))
toyears(daycount("30E/360"), term(90, "days"))
```

`with_daycount()` evaluates operations between Terms with different units.

```{r}
with_daycount("business/252", term(1, "month") + term(12, "days"))
with_daycount("actual/360", term(6, "months") == term(180, "days"))
```

The article [Working with Terms](term.html) has more about Terms.

## Things to watch

**The daycount and the calendar must agree.**
For `actual/...` and `business/...` the days come from the calendar, so an
`actual/360` rate with the `"Brazil/ANBIMA"` calendar counts business days,
and gives a smaller factor than the `actual/360` rate above.

```{r}
compound(spotrate(0.10, "simple", "actual/360", "Brazil/ANBIMA"), d1, d2)
```

Use the `"actual"` calendar with `actual/...` daycounts, and a business
calendar with `business/...`.

**Rates with different daycounts can't be combined.**
Arithmetic and comparison between two SpotRates require the same
compounding, daycount and calendar.
Convert one of them first, as in "Equivalent rates".

```{r}
sr1 <- spotrate(0.10, "discrete", "business/252", "Brazil/ANBIMA")
sr2 <- spotrate(0.10, "discrete", "actual/365", "actual")
try(sr1 - sr2)
```

**Only 30E/360 is supported among the 30/360 variants.**
The US (NASD) and ISDA versions treat the end of the month differently, and
`daycount()` rejects them.

```{r}
try(daycount("30/360"))
```

**Dates of a curve use the calendar.**
The terms of a `SpotRateCurve` are kept in days, and functions that turn them
into dates, like `maturities()`, use the calendar of the curve, even with
`30E/360`.
